analysis.one_liner: Charges oil companies royalties and fees on royalty-free deepwater Gulf leases and sends the money to Gulf coastal states and deficit reduction.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in the final weeks of 2006 with one cosponsor, never received a committee vote and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: Two Gulf of Mexico lease sales in 1998 and 1999 gave deep-water drillers royalty relief without price limits, meaning some companies drilled federal waters without paying royalties even when oil prices were high. This bill would have required the Interior Department to add price thresholds to those leases, so royalties kick in above roughly $35 per barrel, and would have charged a $9-per-barrel fee on royalty-free production above that price. The money would go to Gulf producing states and coastal communities, capped at $5.45 billion through 2016, with any leftover going to deficit reduction. The bill also declared Congress's intent to support American manufacturing and jobs in offshore energy, and included a narrow carve-out for certain high-achieving foreign individuals from U.S. laws that extend to the outer Continental Shelf.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, through deficit reduction, and Gulf producing states and coastal communities, which would receive up to $5.45 billion in royalty revenue over ten years to spend on coastal needs. The bill's statement of intent also aims any new offshore industrial activity toward American workers and manufacturers.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Secretary to amend 1998-1999 Gulf leases to add price thresholds, so companies must start paying royalties once oil tops $34.73 per barrel or gas tops $4.34 per million Btu [S2][S3].
Imposes a conservation fee of $9 per barrel of oil and $1.25 per million Btu of gas on leases with deep-water royalty relief that are not paying royalties above those prices [S2][S3].

Deposits the recovered royalties in a Treasury account, capped at $5.45 billion for fiscal years 2007-2016, for Gulf producing states and coastal communities, with any remainder going to deficit reduction [S2][S3].

Declares Congress's intent that offshore energy development employ American workers and support American manufacturing, including monitoring of personnel and material deployed on the Outer Continental Shelf [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies holding the 1998-1999 deep-water Gulf leases would pay royalties and fees they had been avoiding; some of that cost could eventually show up in energy prices, though the bill itself does not change drilling rights.

drawbacks.text: By requiring the Secretary to agree to any lessee request to amend leases, the bill sets the terms of a government-industry dispute in statute rather than leaving it to negotiation, and it may be a better deal than the companies would otherwise get [S3].
The fee and thresholds apply only to royalty-relief leases producing above the price thresholds, so the companies pay nothing on production below them [S3].

The bill includes a carve-out exempting foreign individuals of 'extraordinary ability' from the U.S. laws extended to the Outer Continental Shelf, a narrow favor that has nothing to do with the bill's revenue purpose [S3].
Its sense-of-Congress language encourages expanded offshore development, which carries environmental risks to Gulf coast communities even as the bill sends them royalty money [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is a good one for taxpayers: recovering royalties from leases that were drafted without price limits, with the money split between coastal communities and deficit reduction. The design is imperfect — it locks in terms favorable enough that lessees would volunteer for them, and it smuggles in an unrelated carve-out for certain foreign individuals — but the drawbacks are modest next to the revenue at stake.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the closing weeks of the 109th Congress, referred to committee and then to a subcommittee, and it expired without a vote when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Charlie Melancon introduced the bill on December 6, 2006, with Rep. Neil Abercrombie as cosponsor [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced [S5].
On December 14, 2006, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, where it sat [S5].
No committee action, floor vote, or further step ever occurred before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil companies holding the 1998-1999 royalty-relief leases kept producing without paying royalties under this bill's terms. Taxpayers and Gulf coastal communities gained nothing from this bill itself, although Congress did address the same leases in a separate Gulf energy law enacted later that December.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies with royalty-free Gulf leases

for.name: Rep. Charlie Melancon
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to add price thresholds and fees to the 1998-99 deepwater Gulf leases.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee on December 14, 2006, and never held a markup or sent it to the floor before the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Richard Pombo
against.role: Chair, House Natural Resources Committee (109th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Led the committee that took no further action on the bill after subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan split appears in the record.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers with 1998-99 deepwater Gulf leases
industries.note: These companies would have to pay royalties above price thresholds plus a $9-per-barrel fee on royalty-free production — costs that currently stay with the companies. Their interest in the bill ran directly against the public's recovery of federal revenue.

industries.industry: Offshore drilling and energy services firms
industries.note: The bill's intent language backs expanded Outer Continental Shelf development aimed at American manufacturing and jobs, which would enlarge the offshore industry, but producers bear the new fees.

industries.industry: Gulf producing state and coastal governments
industries.note: They would receive up to $5.45 billion in royalty revenue over fiscal years 2007-2016 for coastal needs.
